thesis: Language reasoning must preserve epistemic context, alternatives and relations; task-specific compression should remain revisable from richer memory.
role: Chapters 14–18 apply the formal principles to language, neural representations and prediction.

ideas.statement: Texts propose interpretations rather than validated facts; events, roles, temporal contexts and provenance must retain separate statuses.
Packed alternatives share common reasoning without premature pronoun resolution; dependencies must prevent mixing incompatible worlds.
Semirings distinguish alternatives and composition; derivation counts, world counts and probabilities differ, and provenance retains alternative support.
Time, persistence, explicit negation, quantifier scope, reported beliefs and causal intervention require their own contracts.
Symbolic, neural and distributed are not exclusive camps; compare exactness, explicitness and representation axes with fixed memory and error budgets.
Exact computational sufficiency, sound approximation and predictive sufficiency differ; bottleneck compression only preserves specified targets under assumptions.
Preserve sources and richer memory separately from question-specific views so rare exceptions and new questions can reopen discarded distinctions.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: Possession after a transfer does not establish ownership or that a key was used to enter a library.
The ambiguous pronoun can be irrelevant to possession yet essential to identifying who leaves.
Withdrawing one source need not withdraw a conclusion if independent support remains.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: No complete verifier exists for every open-language claim; partial checks need explicit limits.
Statistical prediction does not establish intervention effects.
Shared grammars do not guarantee cheap unrestricted semantics.

audit.notes: Read every unit; preserve proposed versus demonstrated status.
